pedagogy.summary: Because area is additive, a rectilinear figure (an L- or T-shape) can be cut into non-overlapping rectangles, each area found by multiplying, then summed. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing side from the outer measurements. It is a direct application of area-as-additive and of finding rectangle areas by multiplying.
bestPractices: Physically cut or draw the figure into rectangles before calculating, so the decomposition is concrete
Show that more than one valid decomposition gives the SAME total — the point of additivity
Teach how to derive missing internal lengths from the given outer lengths (e.g. 5 − 3 = 2)
Insist the two pieces are non-overlapping — shade them different colours and check no tile is both
Keep square units on every sub-area and the total
keyRepresentations: An L/T-shape with dashed decomposition lines
A grid overlay for counting/checking sub-rectangles
The two sub-rectangles pulled apart and labelled
A figure with some sides blank, prompting missing-length reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Treats the figure as one big rectangle — multiplies the outer bounding dimensions as if the notch weren't there
Overlaps the two sub-rectangles and double-counts the shared corner
Cannot find a sub-rectangle's side when it isn't printed
Adds side lengths / a perimeter-like total instead of areas, or drops the square unit

learn.summary: Teaches children to find the area of compound rectilinear shapes (L- and T-shapes) by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles, finding each rectangle's area by multiplying, and summing. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing internal side from the given outer measurements. This rests on two prior ideas: area is additive, and rectangle area is found by multiplying rows by columns. For the worked example, a 3 m × 5 m rectangle gives 15 m² and a 2 m × 4 m rectangle gives 8 m², summing to 23 m². The sub-areas are ADDED (not multiplied) because area is additive.

activities.title: Cut the L-shaped floor plan into rectangles
feedback: If a cut leaves the corner region inside both pieces, that overlap is double-counted — shade the two pieces in different colours and check that no tile is both colours.
If the child multiplies the two sub-areas (e.g. 15×8) instead of adding, point back to the grid: each rectangle covers a separate set of tiles, so the tile counts are summed, giving 15 + 8 = 23.
If the total differs after a second split, re-check for a gap or overlap: valid non-overlapping splits must give the same total.
If the answer is written as '23 m' rather than '23 m²', relabel: area is counted in square units, not length units.
activities.rationale: Decomposing is a spatial act with concrete consequences: an overlapping cut double-counts the shared corner, and a different valid cut lands on the same total. Drawing and re-cutting makes additivity something the child discovers, and prompting why the pieces are added (not multiplied) names the additive principle explicitly.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
Area is additive: the area of the union of two regions that overlap only at their boundaries is the sum of their areas; area is measured by tiling without gaps or overlaps.
Pupils find the area of rectilinear/compound shapes by counting or by splitting into rectangles at Key Stage 2.
learnerActions: Look at an L-shaped room on a grid with its outer measurements labelled.
Draw a cut line to split the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles.
Find each sub-rectangle's area by multiplying its sides (e.g. 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m²).
Add the two areas to get the total, keeping square-metre units (23 m²).
Say why the two areas are ADDED rather than multiplied: each rectangle covers a separate part of the floor, and area is additive.
Re-cut the same shape a different valid way and confirm the total is still 23 m².
activities.intendedInsight: A rectilinear figure can be split into non-overlapping rectangles whose areas ADD to the whole; the pieces are summed (not multiplied) because area is additive, and any valid split gives the same total.

activities.title: Find the hidden internal side
feedback: If the child stalls at the blank side, prompt: 'Which outer measurements tell you this hidden length?'
If a number is invented rather than computed, show the subtraction that produces it (e.g. 5 − 3 = 2 for that illustrative figure, or 5 − 2 = 3 / 7 − 3 = 4 for the 23 m² plan).
activities.rationale: Deriving missing internal lengths is a distinct hurdle from partitioning; isolating it as a strategy prompt (not a concept reteach) targets children who freeze at an unprinted side.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
learnerActions: Look at a compound shape (which may be a separate illustrative figure, not the earlier floor plan) where one internal side is left blank and only the outer measurements are printed.

Work out which outer measurements determine the missing internal length by subtracting; for example, 5 − 3 = 2 is a generic illustration of taking one printed outer length from another, not the derivation of a hidden side in the 23 m² floor plan (whose hidden sides come from 5 − 2 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4).
Mark the derived length on the figure.
Complete the decomposition and compute the total area.
activities.intendedInsight: A sub-rectangle's unlabelled side can be derived by reasoning about the outer lengths, not guessed or taken only from printed numbers.

activities.title: Spot the whole-rectangle error
feedback: If the child accepts 35 m², overlay a grid and count the corner tiles that are missing from the figure.
If the child multiplies every printed number, ask which rectangle each number belongs to; the shape is two separate rectangles, not one product.
Reinforce: cut the figure into rectangles, then multiply each piece, then add.
activities.rationale: The whole-rectangle error (treating a compound shape as one big rectangle, or multiplying all numbers) is the signature misconception; confronting it on a fresh case surfaces and corrects it. Grid counting grounds the point concretely.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Examine a worked solution where someone multiplied the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7 = 35 m²) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplied every printed number together.
Explain what that person forgot about the shape.
Overlay or imagine a grid and count: the tiles in the missing corner are not there.
Give the correct total by decomposing first (15 + 8 = 23 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the outer bounding dimensions — or multiplying all the printed numbers together — counts tiles the shape does not contain; the missing notch must be accounted for, and here we do that by decomposing the shape into rectangles before multiplying each piece.

activities.title: Covering versus going around
feedback: If the child sums the edges, tile a sub-rectangle and have them count the square units inside instead.
If the square unit is dropped, relabel the total with m².
activities.rationale: Some children add side lengths or drop the square unit, conflating area with perimeter. Contrasting covering with going around, and counting actual tiles, distinguishes the two quantities.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Tile one sub-rectangle and count the square units inside it.
Contrast that with tracing around the edges of the whole figure.
State whether the task asks for area (tiles inside) or perimeter (distance around), and answer with the correct square units.
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts the squares covering the inside and is reported in square units; adding up the edges gives a perimeter-like total, which is a different quantity.

constraints: Insist the two pieces are non-overlapping — shade them different colours and check no tile belongs to both; non-overlapping is exactly what lets the areas add.
Keep square units on every sub-area and on the total.

A static tap-to-reveal figure (reveal the dashed split, then each sub-area, then a lift-the-flap total) can explain the method, but does not let the child attempt their own cut or catch an overlap they created; use it as an explanatory scaffold, not as the main construction task.
Keep the figures flat rectilinear plans. Adding a third dimension drifts toward volume and obscures the decomposition, so a 3D treatment is not suited to this specific objective.

A scripted in-role dialogue does not itself elicit the child drawing a cut, computing each sub-area and summing; if used, let it frame or discuss the task rather than replace the hands-on construction. This is a scope note, not a claim that dialogue is inherently unable to teach the procedure.

Recognition-only formats (matching a shape to a valid decomposition, picking the 35 m² distractor) can assess and reinforce, but do not by themselves elicit the child independently drawing a cut and deriving a missing length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 3×5 = 15, 2×4 = 8, 15+8 = 23 m²; the whole-rectangle distractor 5×7 = 35 m² is intentionally the wrong answer and must never be presented as correct. The 23 m² figure is self-consistent with a 5 m × 7 m bounding box (35 m²) and a 3 m × 4 m notch (12 m²), since 35 − 12 = 23.

The derived length '5 − 3 = 2' is a generic illustration only. In the specific 23 m² figure the hidden internal sides derive as 5 − 2 = 3 or 7 − 3 = 4, so if 'Find the hidden internal side' is deployed on the same shape its numbers must be relabelled for consistency.

Teachers should ensure the printed outer measurements of any specific figure are self-consistent with the intended decomposition, the one blank internal side, and the bounding box used for the distractor before use.
The objective covers both L- and T-shapes; the activities use an L-shape as the representative worked figure, and a T-shaped plan is an equally valid example to vary with.
One cited claim (National Curriculum KS2) was marked unverified in the source; it is retained as supporting the general splitting-into-rectangles approach, not as independent evidence of efficacy.

probeDeeper: 'You split it into these two rectangles — could you split it a different way and still get 23 m²? Show me.' (additivity / conservation across decompositions)
'How did you work out this side when it wasn't written on the plan?'
'Someone got 35 m² by doing 5×7. What did they forget about the shape?' (surfaces the whole-rectangle error on a fresh case)
'Why do we ADD the two areas together, and not multiply them?'
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a decomposition into two non-overlapping rectangles, derives the unlabelled internal length from the given outer lengths, computes 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m², sums to 23 m² keeping square-metre units, and can show that a different valid split gives the same 23 m².

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the whole figure as one rectangle — multiplies the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplies all the given numbers together
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay a grid and count — the tiles in the missing corner aren't there; then cut the figure into rectangles before multiplying.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 35 m² (5×7) for the L-shape, or multiplies every printed number

errorPatterns.pattern: Overlaps the two sub-rectangles and double-counts the shared corner, so the total comes out too big
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't just correct the number — have them shade the two pieces in different colours and check that no tile is both colours; non-overlapping IS what makes the areas add. This coordinates with spatial-structuring practice and self-corrects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two rectangles the child draws share a strip or corner, and that region gets counted in both areas

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot find a sub-rectangle's side when it isn't printed — guesses or freezes rather than deriving it from the outer lengths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'Which outer measurements tell you this hidden length?' and mark the derived length on the figure — a strategy prompt, not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stalls at the blank internal side, or invents a number instead of computing (e.g. 5 − 3)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds side lengths / gives a perimeter-like total instead of areas, or drops the square unit (answers in m not m²)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast covering (tiles inside) with going around (edges); tile one sub-rectangle so the child counts square units and re-labels the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums the edges around the figure, or writes the total as '23 m' rather than '23 m²'

responseLevels.gap: Treats the figure as one rectangle or overlaps the pieces; cannot decompose it into non-overlapping rectangles.
responseLevels.full: Partitions into non-overlapping rectangles (deriving missing internal lengths), sums the areas with correct square units, and recognises that a different valid decomposition yields the same total.
responseLevels.partial: Decomposes into rectangles and finds each area when every dimension is given, but lists the pieces without reliably summing, or stalls when an internal side must be derived — can't yet transfer to a figure needing a worked-out length.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch how the child decomposes. Present an L-shaped room drawn on paper with the outer measurements labelled — overall it is a 3 m × 5 m rectangle with a 2 m × 4 m rectangle joined on, and one internal length is left blank so it must be worked out. Say: 'Find the total area of this room. Show me how you split it up.' Watch them partition, find each area, sum, and handle the missing side; then ask them to split it a different way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child cuts catches overlaps and gaps that a bare answer would hide; the blank internal side catches whether they reason about hidden lengths or just use printed numbers; asking for a second split catches whether they trust additivity or believe the total depends on how you cut.
